evidenceStrength: Current, objective, measurable and independently verifiable.
Approved strategy; signed decision logs; measured benefits; validated metrics; audit/risk evidence.
Supports score 4–5 where outcomes are also visible.
Evidence exists but is partial, inconsistent or dependent on stakeholder judgement.
Draft roadmaps; partially tracked KPIs; limited adoption data; interview consensus.
Usually supports score 2–4 depending on consistency.
Evidence is limited, anecdotal, outdated or not tied to outcomes.
Opinions; informal updates; unsupported claims; old dashboards; unclear ownership.
Should rarely support score above 2 without caveat.
dimensionAnchors: Strategic Alignment
Leaders cannot state the original problem or current outcome; scope has drifted and no current business case exists.
Original rationale is known but outcomes are vague, ownership is unclear, or major scope/funding changes were not re-baselined.
Current strategy and outcomes are documented with owners, but some measures, re-baselining or stop/redirect criteria remain weak.
Investment thesis, outcomes, owners and strategic linkage are current; material changes were explicitly approved and evidence informs funding decisions.
Strategic linkage is continuously tested; measurable outcomes, owners, investment thresholds and stop/redirect criteria are embedded in governance and evidenced over time.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
No current investment thesis or measurable outcome.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 4
Leadership Commitment
Sponsors are nominal; decisions stall, escalations remain unresolved and accountability is unclear.
Leaders attend governance but material decisions are delayed or ownership is fragmented across functions.
Key leaders own outcomes and most decisions are timely, but some constraints or cross-functional accountability gaps remain.
Executives consistently make timely trade-offs, remove constraints and act when evidence weakens confidence.
Leadership accountability is demonstrably embedded; decisions, escalations and corrective actions are traceable, timely and consistently tied to outcomes/value.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Material decisions repeatedly unresolved with no accountable owner.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 5
Technology Readiness
Architecture cannot support required scale/security/resilience; material operational weaknesses are unmanaged.
Core platform works but scaling, resilience, automation, cost or technical debt creates significant uncertainty.
Technology meets current needs with credible plans for remaining scale, resilience, automation or cost gaps.
Architecture, resilience, security, engineering automation and operating economics are proven at the required scale with limited gaps.
Technology is demonstrably scalable, resilient, secure, automated and cost-efficient over time, with technical debt actively governed against business value.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Known scale/security/resilience weakness threatens intended outcome.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 6
People & Culture
Low adoption, unclear roles, missing skills and no credible plan for sustainable behavioural change.
Training/activity exists but adoption is uneven; capacity, incentives or decision rights materially constrain outcomes.
Most required roles, skills and adoption mechanisms exist, but sustainability or behavioural consistency is incomplete.
Adoption is measurable; skills, roles, incentives and decision rights support the target way of working and are embedded in operations.
New behaviours and operating practices are self-sustaining, measurable and continue to improve after programme support reduces.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Capability delivered but target users/processes have not adopted it.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 7
Data & AI Confidence
Critical data lacks ownership; quality is unknown/unreliable; lineage or controls are absent.
Some controls exist but material quality, ownership, lineage or access issues remain unresolved.
Critical data is mostly owned and governed with measured quality, but some gaps or inconsistent definitions remain.
Ownership, quality, lineage, definitions, access and controls are demonstrably effective for material data.
Data is trusted and traceable end-to-end; controls and quality measures are embedded, independently corroborated and consistently support decision-making/value.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Decision-critical data cannot be trusted or traced.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 8
Delivery Excellence
Delivery is unpredictable; quality problems, dependencies and rework dominate and learning is not evident.
Teams deliver outputs but flow, quality or dependencies remain unstable and reporting masks material variability.
Delivery is generally predictable with acceptable quality, but some dependencies, rework or learning loops remain inconsistent.
Flow, cycle time, quality, automation and dependencies are actively measured and demonstrate sustainable predictability.
Delivery system is highly predictable and adaptive; evidence shows continuous improvement, low avoidable rework and rapid learning when assumptions fail.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Persistent quality/dependency problems make outcomes materially unpredictable.
S06 / Dimension anchors / row 9
Business Value Realisation
No reliable benefits baseline or measurable realised value; claims are unsupported.
Some benefits are claimed but attribution, validation, ownership or sustainability is weak.
Material benefits are measured against a baseline with named owners, but some value remains forecast, unvalidated or unevenly realised.
Realised value is measurable, attributable and substantially validated; business owners sustain benefits and the investment case remains credible.
Validated value materially meets/exceeds the investment thesis, is sustained over time and directly informs future funding and portfolio decisions.
Score 3 normally requires some E1/E2 support; scores 4–5 require stronger operating evidence and limited unresolved contradiction.
Reported value is largely asserted/forecast and the investment case cannot be substantiated.

criteria.question: Which original business problem and strategic outcome justified the investment, and do they still hold?
criteria.minimum: Transformation is demonstrably linked to enterprise strategy and the original business problem.

criteria.question: How have scope, spend or priorities changed since approval, and were those changes re-approved against the investment thesis?
criteria.minimum: Current scope, spend and priorities remain consistent with the approved investment thesis.

criteria.question: Which measurable outcomes define success today, and who owns each one?
criteria.minimum: Measurable business outcomes and success measures are explicit.

criteria.question: What evidence would cause you to reduce, redirect or stop investment?
criteria.minimum: Named business owners are accountable for intended outcomes and benefits.

criteria.question: Which material decisions have been delayed in the last two review cycles, and why?
criteria.minimum: Material decisions and trade-offs are made in a timely manner.

criteria.question: Which unresolved escalations or constraints remain open, and who owns resolution?
criteria.minimum: Leaders actively resolve blockers, escalations and resource constraints.

criteria.question: Where is accountability shared, and where does it still fall between functions?
criteria.minimum: Named leaders are accountable for decisions, outcomes and value.

criteria.question: What action followed the last material warning that confidence was weakening?
criteria.minimum: Governance reinforces accountability and acts when confidence weakens.

criteria.question: Can the current architecture support required scale, resilience, security and change velocity?
criteria.minimum: Architecture can support the intended outcome at the required scale.

criteria.question: Which incidents, manual interventions or recovery weaknesses contradict the target-state claim?
criteria.minimum: Reliability, recovery, security and operational controls are adequate.

criteria.question: What evidence shows deployment, automation and engineering practices are sustainable?
criteria.minimum: Deployment, automation and engineering practices support sustainable change.

criteria.question: How are technical debt, dependencies and operating cost affecting the investment case?
criteria.minimum: Operating cost, dependencies and technical debt are understood and managed.

criteria.question: What proportion of target users have adopted the new capability in day-to-day work?
criteria.minimum: New capabilities are used in day-to-day work and adoption is measurable.

criteria.question: Which skills, capacity or incentives are still missing?
criteria.minimum: Required skills, capacity and capability exist or have credible plans.

criteria.question: Which roles, accountabilities or decision rights changed because of the transformation?
criteria.minimum: Roles, accountability and decision rights support the target operating model.

criteria.question: Would the new way of working continue if the programme closed tomorrow?
criteria.minimum: Behaviours and ways of working are changing and can persist after programme closure.

criteria.question: Who owns the critical data and which quality measures demonstrate trust?
criteria.minimum: Critical data has clear ownership and accountability.

criteria.question: Which material data issues remain unresolved and how do they affect the decision?
criteria.minimum: Material data quality is measured, visible and actively managed.

criteria.question: Can a material executive measure be traced through definitions, lineage and source?
criteria.minimum: Definitions, metadata and lineage support traceability and trust.

criteria.question: Are access, governance and controls appropriate for the intended use?
criteria.minimum: Access, governance and controls are appropriate for intended use.

criteria.question: How predictable are flow, cycle time and release outcomes across recent review periods?
criteria.minimum: Delivery flow and cycle time demonstrate sufficient predictability.

criteria.question: Do defect, incident and rework trends support claims of improving quality?
criteria.minimum: Release quality, defects and incidents show sustainable engineering discipline.

criteria.question: Which dependencies repeatedly change delivery outcomes or create delay?
criteria.minimum: Dependencies, rework and delivery risks are visible and actively managed.

criteria.question: What changed after recent assumptions proved wrong, and what evidence shows learning?
criteria.minimum: Teams adapt when assumptions fail and improve delivery over time.

criteria.question: Which benefits are validated, which remain forecast or asserted, and against what baseline?
criteria.minimum: Approved benefits case and baseline are clear and current.

criteria.question: What measurable value exists today and what portion is attributable to this investment?
criteria.minimum: Realised financial, customer, productivity, revenue, cost or risk outcomes are evidenced.

criteria.question: Where is the organisation operating differently because of the delivered capability?
criteria.minimum: Material benefits are attributable to the investment and validated where relevant.

criteria.question: Who owns benefits after the programme ends, and how will value continue to be measured?
criteria.minimum: Named business owners remain accountable for benefits after programme delivery.

sourceText: TCI™ gives leaders a structured view of whether the conditions exist for a major technology, AI or business change programme to produce the value it was funded to deliver.
The assessment connects the original case for investment with current delivery evidence, business outcomes and the issues that need executive attention.
Start with the original business problem and expected outcome.
Assess business, technology, data, people, delivery and leadership together.
Focus findings on decisions leaders need to make.
Repeat the assessment over time to show whether confidence is changing.
Each dimension receives a plain-English confidence judgement. Numerical scoring should only be introduced once the scoring method has been tested against real assessments.
Every material finding should state what evidence supports it, where evidence is incomplete and where the assessment relies on management or stakeholder assertion.
Use source evidence that can be traced back to a document, metric, decision record or interview.
Seek corroboration for material claims where practical.
Record missing evidence as a finding when it affects the decision.
Keep the detailed evidence classification scheme in the separate TCI™ Evidence Classification Standard.
TCI™ supports executive judgement. The assessment should make clear which decision paths the evidence supports:
Executive judgement: the overall confidence view and why.
TCI™ profile: judgement across all 7 dimensions.
Evidence summary: what is established, uncertain or missing.
Value view: value realised, value at risk and material assumptions.
Decision considerations: the choices leaders need to address.
Priority actions: a short list of issues that would materially change confidence.
The assessment owner must be independent of day-to-day programme delivery.
Material conflicts of interest must be disclosed.
Akeel Advisory's fee must not depend on the direction of the conclusion.
Specialist legal, cyber, regulatory, audit or technical opinions should be provided by suitably qualified specialists when required.
Executive management and the Board retain accountability for investment decisions.

Version 1.0 is the working method for pilot use. The next step is to test it on real or historical programmes, tighten the evidence rules, and only then decide whether numerical scoring and benchmark comparisons add useful decision information.
Core question: How confident should we be that this investment will deliver sustainable business value?
Strategic Alignment | Is the investment still tied to a clear business problem and strategic outcome?
Leadership Commitment | Are leaders accountable for decisions, outcomes and value?
Technology Readiness | Can the technology support the intended outcome at the required scale and cost?
People & Culture | Are the roles, skills, behaviours and adoption conditions in place?
Data Confidence | Is the data trusted, owned, governed and fit for the intended use?
Delivery Excellence | Can the organisation turn investment into working capability with sufficient predictability and quality?
Business Value Realisation | Is measurable value being realised and does the investment case still hold?
1. Frame | Confirm the decision to be supported, scope, investment, expected outcomes and key stakeholders.
2. Gather | Review the business case, investment papers, plans, metrics, risks, benefits evidence and relevant technical material.
3. Test | Interview selected leaders and delivery teams. Check material claims against available evidence.
4. Assess | Review each TCI™ dimension and record strengths, gaps, uncertainty and dependencies.
5. Judge | Form an overall view of transformation confidence. Explain what is driving that view.
6. Decide | Set out the decision paths supported by the evidence and the issues leaders should resolve.
7. Reassess | Repeat at an agreed point to test whether confidence has improved, weakened or remained unchanged.
Strong | Evidence supports confidence in the current position.
Conditional | The case remains credible, with material conditions that need attention.
Weak | Material gaps reduce confidence in the current position.
Insufficient evidence | A reliable judgement can't yet be made.
Invest more | Evidence supports further investment or expansion.
Correct | The investment case remains credible, but specific conditions need action.
Reset | Material assumptions, scope or approach need to be reconsidered.
Stop | Evidence no longer gives sufficient confidence for continued investment.
Reassess | More evidence or time is needed before a major decision.

Use this guide to decide what evidence matters in a TCI™ assessment. The test is simple: does the evidence show that the organisation is becoming more capable and more likely to create sustainable business value?
Evidence will vary by programme. Use the examples below as a guide, then test them against the investment case and the decision leaders need to make.
Is the work still tied to enterprise strategy and measurable outcomes?
Are leaders making decisions, owning outcomes and removing constraints?
Is the technology estate becoming easier to change, secure and operate?
Are skills, behaviour and ways of working changing with the technology?
Can leaders trust the data used for decisions and AI?
Can teams produce quality outcomes predictably and sustainably?

Trace material findings back to a document, metric, decision record or interview.
Use operating evidence where possible. A programme report alone may not show whether capability or value has changed.
Check material claims with more than 1 source where practical.
Record missing evidence when it affects the judgement.
Keep evidence, management assertion and assessor judgement separate.
Do not let a strong overall picture hide 1 weak dimension that could threaten the investment case.
For each dimension, record the current confidence judgement, the evidence behind it, the main gap or uncertainty, and what would need to change before confidence rises.
